Deterministically compiled from canonical evidence. Importance measures impact, not truth; evidence/confidence remain separate.

blocks.text: 1. FrontierPhysics benchmarks end-to-end AI-agent research across nine physics domains

Desk: evaluation_science Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · developing · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If the reported evaluation is sound, a multi-domain benchmark built from active physicists’ own open-ended research could materially change how scientific-agent capability is measured and expose the gap between task correctness and publishable research. The score reflects that consequence, not confidence in the paper’s results.

What changed: A 4 November arXiv preprint introduces FrontierPhysics, an end-to-end benchmark built from physicists’ own research projects. The authors report 56 tasks from 42 physicists across nine domains, with agents required to plan research, run analyses or experiments, and produce verifiable outputs and manuscripts. Across 22 models and 26 configurations, they report pass rates below 30%; Claude Opus 5.5 is highest at 27.4%. The authors also report manually correcting nine false failures among 168 GPT-6 Astra xhigh rollouts. These are paper-reported results, not an independent rerun. Why it matters: The benchmark tests whether agents can carry a multi-stage research project through to a correct, defensible manuscript, rather than solve a fixed problem or reproduce a supplied paper. If its task curation and grading prove robust, it could sharpen capability comparisons and expose where agents still need expert judgment. The current evidence supports reporting the benchmark and its authors’ results, not a general conclusion that today’s agents can or cannot perform scientific research.
Demonstrated: The arXiv submission and the paper’s reported methods and results are verified as published claims. No benchmark outcome was independently reproduced here.

Claimed: Authors report 56 end-to-end tasks from 42 physicists across nine physics domains; evaluation of 22 models in 26 configurations; highest Pass@1 of 27.4% for Claude Opus 5.5; and a corrected 20.2% pass rate (34/168) for GPT-6 Astra xhigh after manual correction of nine false failures.

Mechanism: Each task begins from an open research prompt based on a contributor’s own project. Agents must investigate literature, plan and conduct research, and produce numerical artifacts plus a manuscript. The benchmark combines deterministic verifiers with task-specific expert rubrics; failure analysis includes manual review.

Strongest baseline: The paper compares its benchmark design with earlier physics and scientific-agent benchmarks; results are within its own FrontierPhysics v0.1 tasks and should not be treated as a matched universal capability ranking.

Regime: Physics only: 56 tasks across nine domains; 22 models in 26 configurations; three trials per model-task and a 10-hour timeout cap per rollout. The study uses different agent harnesses and shared reviewer settings as described by the authors.

Limitations: All benchmark performance numbers are author-reported in an arXiv preprint and were not independently reproduced in this activation.; The same reviewer model, GPT-5.6 Sol, graded all rollouts; the paper reports a Claude Opus 5.5 regrade was more lenient on its own model family.; The paper reports nine false failures corrected during manual review of GPT-6 Astra xhigh rollouts, showing that the benchmark’s error rate and pass counts are sensitive to evaluation review.; This physics task sample does not establish performance on other scientific disciplines or real-world research programs.

Open evidence gaps: No independent reproduction or external audit of the task set, rubric judgments or model pass rates was inspected.; Although the paper says workspace and trajectory files are collected for Hugging Face datasets, this activation did not identify or inspect the corresponding public dataset and code release.

items: SpecCompact reports faster agent context compaction through parallel semantic verification — importance 5/10 · A 4 November arXiv preprint introduces SpecCompact, which fine-tunes a small drafter to generate six context-summary slots in parallel and uses a target model to verify and repair proposed lines. The authors report 2.04–5.63× compaction-latency speedups over Hermes-style summarization across AppWorld and τ³ with Gemma4-31B-IT and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B. A separate Hermes/Gemma4 deployment study reports an 8.68× median paired speedup across three author-designed scenarios. These are paper-reported measurements. The paper says the method does not provide a consistent accuracy advantage; task-performance results vary by model and benchmark, and the full task evaluation did not use all system optimizations. — FCMO-9BCDCE82CB25

FrontierPhysics benchmarks end-to-end AI-agent research across nine physics domains — importance 6/10 · A 4 November arXiv preprint introduces FrontierPhysics, an end-to-end benchmark built from physicists’ own research projects. The authors report 56 tasks from 42 physicists across nine domains, with agents required to plan research, run analyses or experiments, and produce verifiable outputs and manuscripts. Across 22 models and 26 configurations, they report pass rates below 30%; Claude Opus 5.5 is highest at 27.4%. The authors also report manually correcting nine false failures among 168 GPT-6 Astra xhigh rollouts. These are paper-reported results, not an independent rerun. — FCMO-29E5B5C6B4FC

MCPGuard paper reports conformance gaps in official Model Context Protocol SDKs — importance 5/10 · An arXiv preprint presents MCPGuard, a method that compares the Model Context Protocol specification with official SDK models and session logic, then checks candidate gaps with executable proof-of-concept tests. On Python SDK 1.26.0 and TypeScript SDK 1.29.0, the authors report 13 and 19 confirmed gaps, including 27 structural findings and five behavioral findings. They also report that two malformed URI-format metadata fields were accepted by all 32 public servers that completed the study’s handshake test. The authors say findings were privately reported to maintainers. These are paper-reported results, not an independent audit of current releases. ArXiv’s abstract page and Atom API date v1 to 12 August 2026, while its 4 November cs.AI new-submissions list includes the paper; why the listing contains it remains unresolved, so 4 November is not treated as the paper’s established first-publication date. — FCMO-C7551624199B

A paper proposes auditability as a fourth machine-unlearning criterion and reports a two-stage method with dataset tradeoffs — importance 4/10 · The Nov. 4 arXiv preprint “Widen the Gap, Hide the Gap” treats auditability—whether a provider can distinguish requested-forget examples from retained examples under a chosen statistic—as a fourth criterion for machine unlearning. It proposes GapWiden, which trains an audit-statistic gap into the unlearned model, and GapVeil, an inference-time rejection sampler intended to reduce disclosure of that gap. The authors report evaluations over eleven unlearning methods on TOFU and MUSE. Results are paper-reported: auditability rises toward 0.99 on MUSE, but retain performance on MUSE News falls from 0.569 to 0.380. These benchmark results do not establish deletion from a deployed model or proof of deletion for an individual request. — FCMO-303DC579C475

Anthropic reports a bacteriophage-derived vault structure and engineered nanocapsule — importance 5/10 · Anthropic reports the first cryo-EM structure of a vault-like particle formed by a bacteriophage protein in a prokaryotic laboratory system. In its 4 November article, the company says its team searched about 15 billion predicted proteins, tested 15 candidates, observed seven vault-like assemblies, and confirmed four by cryo-EM. It describes a 96-copy phage-derived structure and an engineered variant with about 20% more enclosed volume. Anthropic also reports that Claude helped with sequence search, construct design, isolation-method development and microscopy processing under human direction; a purification workflow took about 90 minutes rather than about three days. These are first-party claims. The particles were made in E. coli; their natural function and formation in native hosts remain unknown, and the linked technical report and independent reproduction were not available in this review. — FCMO-68F60B43525B

China’s central science-industry integration opinion directs enterprise-led research and AI+ deployment — importance 5/10 · On Oct 21, 2026, China’s CPC Central Committee General Office and State Council General Office issued an opinion on deeper integration of science and industrial innovation. The text calls for enterprise-led applied research projects, staged funding and milestone evaluation, technology-transfer mechanisms, demonstration scenarios, broader private-enterprise access to research facilities and data, and full implementation of AI+ across industries. This record covers the issued policy and its stated mechanisms; it does not establish implementation, dedicated budgets, adoption or measured effects. — FCMO-745918193FB7
